claims.text: Adjusting the relative concentrations of Fe, Co, Mn, and P will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability relative to the baseline composition.
Adjusting the relative concentrations of Fe, Co, Mn, and P will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to the baseline composition.
Increasing phosphorus content while adjusting transition-metal levels is a candidate compositional intervention.
The intervention is expected to be effective when the alloy is processed by arc solidification and rapid melt spinning.
The intervention will be effective only within a limited range of Fe, Co, Mn, and P ratios.
Optimized elemental ratios will increase atomic-size mismatch.
Optimized elemental ratios will enhance configurational entropy.
Increased atomic-size mismatch and configurational entropy will kinetically hinder crystallization.
The compositional intervention will increase atomic disorder.
The compositional intervention will enhance chemical short-range order.
Increased atomic disorder and chemical short-range order will suppress crystalline-phase nucleation during cooling.
Increased atomic disorder and chemical short-range order will suppress crystalline-phase growth during cooling.
Suppressing nucleation and crystal growth will lower the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
Suppressing nucleation and crystal growth will raise the crystallization onset temperature.
The optimized composition will have a lower critical cooling rate than the baseline under comparable processing conditions.
The optimized composition will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline.
Moving the phosphorus or transition-metal proportions too far from the baseline may diminish or reverse the benefit through other structural instabilities.
The predicted benefit may be specific to rapid-solidification processing at high cooling rates.
